Present and future climate: CHELSA, lapse-rate downscaling and canopy buffering

geo-climate.Rd

Climate inputs for range-shift models. Unlike the deprecated geo_chelsa(), which downloads whole global files, these read only the area needed, and future climate comes from CHELSA-CMIP6 itself.

  • geo_chelsa_area() reads CHELSA V2.1 climatologies (Karger et al. 2017), about 1 km, for an area: the 1981-2010 baseline or CMIP6 projections for 2011-2040, 2041-2070 and 2071-2100 under SSP1-2.6, SSP3-7.0 and SSP5-8.5 from five global climate models (GCMs). Only the window over the area is read from the cloud-optimised files; scale and offset are applied, so temperatures are in degrees C.

  • geo_downscale_lapse() brings a coarse temperature layer down to the resolution of a fine digital elevation model with a lapse rate: $$T_{fine} = T_{coarse} + \gamma (z_{coarse} - z_{fine}) / 1000,$$ where \(z_{coarse}\) is the elevation the coarse value represents (by default the mean of the fine DEM within each coarse cell) and \(\gamma\) the lapse rate in degrees C per km. On steep tropical mountains a 1 km cell can span over 1,000 m, about 5 degrees C, so this step matters for species with narrow elevational ranges.

  • geo_canopy_offset() adds the buffering of the forest canopy: below closed forest, maximum temperatures are lower and minimum temperatures higher than in the open (De Frenne et al. 2019, 2021). The offset is scaled by canopy cover (0 to 1), for example from geo_landcover().

Usage

geo_chelsa_area(
  area,
  variables = "bio1",
  period = "1981-2010",
  gcm = NULL,
  ssp = NULL
)

geo_chelsa_urls(
  variables = "bio1",
  period = "1981-2010",
  gcm = NULL,
  ssp = NULL
)

geo_downscale_lapse(climate, dem, lapse_rate, coarse_dem = NULL)

geo_canopy_offset(temperature, canopy, offset)

Arguments

area

Area: sf, SpatRaster, SpatVector, SpatExtent or c(xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax) in degrees.

variables

CHELSA variables, for example "bio1" (annual mean temperature), "bio5" (maximum temperature of the warmest month), "bio6", "bio12" (annual precipitation).

period

"1981-2010" (baseline), "2011-2040", "2041-2070" or "2071-2100".

gcm, ssp

For future periods: GCMs ("gfdl-esm4", "ipsl-cm6a-lr", "mpi-esm1-2-hr", "mri-esm2-0", "ukesm1-0-ll") and scenarios ("ssp126", "ssp370", "ssp585"). Every combination is read, giving an ensemble.

climate

Coarse temperature SpatRaster (one or more layers).

dem

Fine elevation SpatRaster (metres); the result has its grid.

lapse_rate

Temperature lapse rate in degrees C per km (positive: cooler with height). Use one measured on your mountain where possible; about 5 to 6.5 is typical of humid tropical mountains.

coarse_dem

Elevation that the coarse values represent; by default the mean of dem within each cell of climate.

temperature

Temperature SpatRaster (degrees C).

canopy

Canopy cover SpatRaster, 0 (open) to 1 (closed forest), or a logical forest layer.

offset

Temperature difference below closed canopy relative to the open, in degrees C: one number, or a SpatRaster. There is no default because it depends on the variable: forests cool maximum temperatures by about 4 degrees C on average and warm minimum temperatures by about 1 degree C (De Frenne et al. 2019), with larger offsets in dense tropical forest. Use a value measured with loggers where possible.

Value

geo_chelsa_area(): a SpatRaster with one layer per variable (and GCM and scenario), named for example "bio1_2071-2100_mpi-esm1-2-hr_ssp585".

geo_chelsa_urls(): a tibble of name and url of the files geo_chelsa_area() would read (no download).

geo_downscale_lapse(): a SpatRaster on the grid of dem.

geo_canopy_offset(): temperature + canopy * offset.

References

De Frenne, P. et al. (2019). Global buffering of temperatures under forest canopies. Nature Ecology & Evolution, 3, 744-749.

De Frenne, P. et al. (2021). Forest microclimates and climate change: importance, drivers and future research agenda. Global Change Biology, 27, 2279-2297.

Karger, D. N. et al. (2017). Climatologies at high resolution for the earth's land surface areas. Scientific Data, 4, 170122.

Examples

if (FALSE) { # interactive() && rlang::is_installed("terra")
huon <- c(146.5, -6.5, 147, -6)
now <- geo_chelsa_area(huon, "bio1")
future <- geo_chelsa_area(huon, "bio1",
  period = "2071-2100",
  gcm = c("mpi-esm1-2-hr", "ukesm1-0-ll"), ssp = "ssp585"
)
warming <- future - now
}
